name: Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali
line: A judge of Basra credited with the dots that first marked the vowels in the mushaf.
story: He embraced Islam in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime but never met him, and later served Ali as judge of Basra. As new Muslims began to slip in Arabic, he is said to have set down its first rules. Tradition credits him with marking the vowels of the mushaf with coloured dots.
legacy: His dots led, through al-Khalil, to the vowel marks printed in every mushaf today.
note: Most accounts say Ali urged him to the task; the details are traditional. His birth year is an estimate.

name: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib
line: The foremost scholar of the generation that learned from the Companions in Madinah.
story: Son-in-law of Abu Hurayrah, he gathered the judgments of Umar and the hadith of the Companions, and is counted first among the Seven Jurists of Madinah. When the caliph Abd al-Malik asked for his daughter for his son, he married her instead to a poor student of his.
legacy: His rulings became a core of the Madinan fiqh that Malik later recorded.
lesson: He preferred a pious poor man to a prince as a son-in-law.
note: Some reports give his death as 93 or 105 AH; 94 AH is the most cited.

name: Urwah ibn al-Zubayr
line: Aisha's nephew, who wrote some of the first accounts of the Prophet's ﷺ campaigns.
story: Son of al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam and Asma bint Abi Bakr, he learned closely from his aunt Aisha and was one of the Seven Jurists of Madinah. His letters answering the caliph Abd al-Malik's questions on the maghazi are among the earliest prose on the seerah. Told he had lost a leg and a son on one journey, he praised God for what remained.
legacy: Al-Zuhri and Ibn Ishaq built the seerah on his reports.

name: Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr
arabic: القاسم بن محمد بن أبي بكر
line: Grandson of Abu Bakr, orphaned young and raised and taught by his aunt Aisha.
story: After his father Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr was killed in Egypt, Aisha took him into her home and taught him. He became one of the Seven Jurists of Madinah, famous for answering 'I do not know' rather than guessing.
legacy: Through his students, Aisha's fiqh flowed into the school of Madinah.
lesson: Saying 'I do not know' is part of knowledge.
note: His death is given as 106, 107 or 108 AH.
wiki: Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr

name: Amrah bint Abd al-Rahman
line: Aisha's ward, whose hadith the caliph Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz ordered to be written down.
story: An orphan of the Ansar raised in Aisha's household, she became the main keeper of Aisha's hadith and rulings. The judges of Madinah consulted her, and at least one changed a verdict after hearing her report. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his governor Abu Bakr ibn Hazm to record her narrations.
legacy: Much of what we know from Aisha reached later books through her.
note: Her death is given as 98 or 103 AH; her birth year is not known.

name: Aisha bint Talhah
line: A granddaughter of Abu Bakr, raised near her aunt Aisha, remembered for learning and eloquence.
story: Daughter of Talhah ibn Ubaydullah and Umm Kulthum bint Abi Bakr, she grew up close to Aisha and narrated hadith from her. She was famed in Madinah for her knowledge, her poetry and her strong character.
note: Dates of her birth and death are uncertain; 101 AH is a common estimate for her death.

name: Umm al-Darda
role: Teacher in the mosque of Damascus
line: A jurist who taught men and women, a caliph among them, in the mosques of Damascus and Jerusalem.
story: Married to the Companion Abu al-Darda, she spent long hours in study and worship. She taught hadith and fiqh in Damascus and Jerusalem, and the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik is reported to have sat in her circle. She said she had sought worship in everything and found none better than sitting with the learned.
legacy: Her circle is an early proof that women taught openly in the great mosques.
note: This is Umm al-Darda the Younger (Hujaymah), a tabi'iyyah; Umm al-Darda the Elder (Khayrah) was a Companion.

name: Hasan al-Basri
line: A tabi'i whose sermons on fearing God and the shortness of life are still quoted.
story: Born in Madinah to a freed maid of Umm Salamah, he grew up among the Companions and settled in Basra. He taught Quran, hadith and fiqh in its mosque and spoke plainly even to the governor al-Hajjaj. Almost every early Sufi chain, and many scholarly ones, pass through him.
legacy: Both the ascetic tradition and the theology circles of Basra trace their beginnings to his gatherings.

name: Muhammad ibn Sirin
line: A Basran scholar famous for strict honesty and for interpreting dreams.
story: The son of a freedman of Anas ibn Malik, he traded cloth and went to prison for a debt rather than cheat. He was among the first to insist on checking chains of narration: 'This knowledge is religion, so look to whom you take your religion from.'
legacy: His saying on checking narrators became a founding principle of hadith criticism.
note: His saying is in the introduction of Sahih Muslim. The popular dream book under his name was compiled later and is not reliably his.

name: Hafsa bint Sirin
role: Quran and hadith scholar of Basra
line: She memorised the Quran at twelve, and her brother Ibn Sirin sent hard questions to her.
story: A sister of Muhammad ibn Sirin, she narrated from the Companion Umm Atiyyah, including her report of the washing of the Prophet's ﷺ daughter. She spent some thirty years in her prayer room. When Ibn Sirin was unsure of a Quranic reading, he would tell people to go and ask Hafsa.
legacy: Her narrations are in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

name: Ata ibn Abi Rabah
line: A Black freedman who became the leading authority on the rites of Hajj.
story: Born in Yemen and raised in Makkah, he was dark-skinned, flat-nosed and later lame, yet he became the mufti of the Sacred Mosque. Ibn Abbas sent questioners to him, and Umayyad caliphs came with their sons to ask him about Hajj and waited their turn.
legacy: His rulings on Hajj fill the later books of fiqh.
lesson: Knowledge and taqwa, not lineage or looks, raised him above kings.

name: Mujahid ibn Jabr
role: Student of Ibn Abbas in tafsir
line: He read the whole Quran to Ibn Abbas, stopping at every verse to ask about it.
story: A freedman of Makkah, he said he went through the Quran with Ibn Abbas three times, asking at each verse when and why it came down. His explanations are among the most quoted in later tafsir works such as al-Tabari's.
legacy: The Makkan school of tafsir rests largely on him.

name: Ikrimah mawla Ibn Abbas
line: A Berber freedman who carried Ibn Abbas's tafsir to many lands.
story: Ibn Abbas taught him the Quran and Sunnah, reportedly binding his feet to keep him at his studies. He travelled widely, to Egypt, Yemen, Khurasan and the Maghreb, and his reports on the meaning of verses run all through the classical commentaries.
note: Scholars differed over him: al-Bukhari accepted his narrations, while Muslim mostly avoided relying on him alone.

name: Sa'id ibn Jubayr
line: A student of Ibn Abbas, executed by al-Hajjaj for joining a revolt against him.
story: A freedman of Kufa, he learned tafsir from Ibn Abbas and was one of its leading scholars. After the failed revolt of Ibn al-Ash'ath he hid for years, then was caught and executed at Wasit. Al-Hajjaj died within months, and tradition says the memory of him haunted the governor.
legacy: His courage before a tyrant became a byword among scholars.

name: Ibrahim al-Nakha'i
line: The jurist of Kufa whose method passed through his student Hammad to Abu Hanifa.
story: He learned from the students of Ibn Masud and visited Aisha as a boy. He became the leading mufti of Kufa, careful to reason from the Quran and Sunnah where no clear text settled a case.
legacy: The Hanafi school stands on his Kufan method.

name: Wahb ibn Munabbih
line: A Yemeni tabi'i who was a main channel of stories about earlier prophets and nations.
story: From a Persian family settled in Yemen, he knew the books of the People of the Book and told many stories of the prophets and ancient kings. Much of this lore reached the tafsir works through him.
legacy: Many names and details in the commentaries' stories of the prophets come from his reports.
note: He was trusted in hadith, but his stories of earlier nations are Isra'iliyyat: neither believed nor denied unless the Quran or Sunnah confirms them. His death is given as 110 or 114 AH.

name: Nafi' mawla Ibn Umar
line: The freedman of Ibn Umar, a link in the 'golden chain' of hadith.
story: Captured in war as a boy, he served Abdullah ibn Umar for some thirty years and absorbed his knowledge. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz sent him to Egypt to teach the Sunnah. Al-Bukhari called 'Malik from Nafi' from Ibn Umar' the soundest chain of all.
legacy: Hundreds of hadith in the Muwatta and the Sahihs come through him.
note: Not the same person as Nafi' al-Madani, the Quran reader.

name: Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri
role: Hadith compiler of the Umayyad age
line: He led the first official effort to write down the hadith, at a caliph's request.
story: A Qurashi of Madinah, he sought hadith from house to house and later served the Umayyad court. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, fearing knowledge would die with its carriers, asked scholars to record the Sunnah, and al-Zuhri led this work. Malik, Ibn Ishaq and many others learned from him.
legacy: The written hadith collections of the next century grew from his notebooks.

name: Ja'far al-Sadiq
line: A descendant of the Prophet ﷺ through Husayn who taught both Abu Hanifa and Malik.
story: Through his mother he also descended from Abu Bakr. He taught in Madinah, and Abu Hanifa and Malik both learned from him. Sunni scholars honour him as a trustworthy imam, while Twelver and Ismaili Shia regard him as the sixth Imam and base their Ja'fari law on his teaching.
legacy: He is one of the few figures revered by Sunnis and Shia alike.
note: His birth is given as 80 or 83 AH. The alchemy later attributed to him through Jabir ibn Hayyan is doubted by historians.

name: Abu Hanifa
line: A Kufan cloth merchant who built the first great school of Islamic law.
story: Of Persian descent, he is said to have seen the Companion Anas ibn Malik as a boy. He traded cloth and taught in Kufa, working through cases with his students by careful reasoning from the Quran, Sunnah and the rulings of the Companions. He refused to serve as judge under the Umayyads and then al-Mansur, and died in prison in Baghdad.
legacy: The Hanafi school became the law of the Abbasids, Ottomans and Mughals and has the most followers today.
note: Reports differ on whether he died in prison or shortly after release; his refusal of the judgeship is widely reported.

name: Malik ibn Anas
line: The imam of Madinah whose Muwatta is one of the oldest surviving books of Islamic law.
story: He studied under Nafi', al-Zuhri and Ja'far al-Sadiq and taught in the Prophet's ﷺ Mosque for decades, so in awe of the city that he would not ride within it. Flogged by a governor for a fatwa the Abbasids disliked, he would not retract it. When the caliph proposed imposing the Muwatta on every province, he declined.
legacy: The Maliki school spread across North and West Africa and al-Andalus.
note: His birth is given as 93, 94 or 97 AH.

name: Al-Awza'i
line: The imam of Syria, remembered for defending civilians against collective punishment.
story: He led the scholars of Syria from Beirut. When an Abbasid governor deported whole Christian villages of Mount Lebanon for a revolt by a few, he wrote in protest that no one may be punished for another's sin, citing the Quran.
legacy: His school was the first law of al-Andalus before the Maliki school replaced it.

name: Al-Layth ibn Sa'd
line: The great jurist of Egypt, whom al-Shafi'i judged more learned than Malik.
story: A wealthy man who gave away his yearly income, he led the scholars of Egypt and exchanged famous letters with Malik on whether the practice of Madinah binds all Muslims. Al-Shafi'i said his students failed to preserve his school.
legacy: His letter to Malik is one of the earliest records of respectful scholarly disagreement.

name: Sufyan al-Thawri
line: Called 'commander of the believers in hadith', he spent his last years hiding from the caliph.
story: He refused posts from the Abbasids and spoke against their injustice, so al-Mansur and al-Mahdi sought him. He died in hiding in Basra. His own school of law had followers for some centuries before fading.

name: Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak
line: A merchant of Merv who spent his wealth on scholars and his summers on the frontier.
story: He travelled to every centre of learning and wrote early books on zuhd and on jihad. He paid for the Hajj of poor companions and gave generously to students. He died at Hit on the Euphrates, returning from the Byzantine frontier.
legacy: His Kitab al-Zuhd is one of the oldest books on detachment from the world.

name: Abu Yusuf
role: First chief judge of the Abbasids
line: Abu Hanifa's student, the first to hold the title of chief judge, under Harun al-Rashid.
story: Raised poor, he was supported by Abu Hanifa through his studies. As chief judge in Baghdad he wrote Kitab al-Kharaj for Harun al-Rashid, advising on taxes, fair treatment of non-Muslim subjects and care of the poor.
legacy: Through him Hanafi law became the law of the Abbasid courts.

name: Muhammad al-Shaybani
line: He wrote down Hanafi law and an early Muslim book on the law of nations.
story: He studied briefly under Abu Hanifa, then Abu Yusuf, and spent three years with Malik in Madinah. His books became the base texts of the Hanafi school, and his Siyar sets out rules for war, treaties and envoys. Al-Shafi'i studied with him in Baghdad.
legacy: He is often called a father of Islamic international law.

name: Al-Shafi'i
line: The jurist who first set down a method for deriving law, in his book al-Risalah.
story: Born in Gaza to a family of Quraysh and raised poor in Makkah, he memorised the Muwatta and studied under Malik. He learned Hanafi law from al-Shaybani in Baghdad, then settled in Egypt. His Risalah explained how the Quran, Sunnah, consensus and analogy fit together.
legacy: Usul al-fiqh begins with him; his school spread through Egypt, Sham, Yemen, East Africa and Southeast Asia.

name: Ahmad ibn Hanbal
line: The imam of Baghdad who would not bend during the Mihna, the inquisition over the Quran.
story: He travelled across the empire collecting hadith and gathered nearly 30,000 in his Musnad. When al-Mamun and his successors demanded that scholars declare the Quran created, he refused, and was flogged and jailed under al-Mu'tasim. Huge crowds attended his funeral in Baghdad.
legacy: The Hanbali school and the Musnad, one of the largest hadith collections, grew from his work.
lesson: He held to the truth when the state itself demanded otherwise.

name: Sahnun
line: The judge of Kairouan whose Mudawwana made North Africa Maliki.
story: He travelled east to learn from Ibn al-Qasim, Malik's student in Egypt, and compiled the Mudawwana, a vast record of Malik's rulings. As judge under the Aghlabids he took no salary and held even the ruler's household to account.
legacy: The Mudawwana became the core text of Maliki law in the Maghreb and al-Andalus.

name: Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi
role: Carrier of the Muwatta to al-Andalus
line: An Andalusian of Berber descent whose copy of the Muwatta is the one read worldwide.
story: He travelled to Madinah as a young man and heard the Muwatta from Malik shortly before Malik's death. Back in Cordoba he became the leading jurist and helped make Maliki law the law of al-Andalus.
legacy: Nearly every printed Muwatta today is his recension.

name: Al-Bukhari
line: A scholar of Bukhara whose Sahih is held to be the most reliable book after the Quran.
story: Orphaned young, he began memorising hadith as a boy and travelled from Khurasan to Egypt to hear them. Over about sixteen years he chose some 7,500 narrations, with repeats, from many thousands, and is said to have prayed two rak'ahs before entering each. He died in exile at Khartank near Samarkand.
legacy: Sahih al-Bukhari is the most studied hadith book in the world.

name: Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj
line: A scholar of Nishapur whose Sahih ranks with al-Bukhari's at the top of hadith books.
story: A cloth merchant, he travelled through Iraq, the Hijaz, Sham and Egypt and studied with al-Bukhari, whom he deeply revered. His Sahih places each hadith together with all its chains, which makes it a favourite of hadith specialists.
legacy: Sahih Muslim, with al-Bukhari's, forms 'the two Sahihs' at the heart of Sunni hadith.
note: His birth is given as 202, 204 or 206 AH.

name: Abu Dawud
line: His Sunan gathered the hadith that jurists rely on for rulings.
story: From Sijistan in eastern Persia, he studied with Ahmad ibn Hanbal and settled in Basra at the governor's request to revive learning there. From the many thousands of hadith he had written, he chose about 4,800 on matters of law.
legacy: Sunan Abu Dawud is one of the six canonical hadith books.

name: Al-Tirmidhi
line: A student of al-Bukhari who graded each hadith and noted how jurists used it.
story: From Tirmidh on the Oxus, he studied with al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud. His Jami' labels each hadith as sound, good or weak and records the views of the schools on it. He also wrote al-Shama'il on the Prophet's ﷺ appearance and manners, and went blind in later life.
legacy: The grade 'hasan' (good) became standard through his book.

name: Al-Nasa'i
line: A strict critic of narrators whose Sunan is one of the six canonical books.
story: Born at Nasa in Khurasan, he lived long in Egypt and was known for demanding standards for narrators. He left Egypt for Damascus late in life and died in 915; reports differ on where he was buried.
legacy: His Sunan is counted among the soundest of the four Sunan books.

name: Ibn Majah
line: A scholar of Qazvin whose Sunan completed the six canonical books.
story: He travelled through Iraq, the Hijaz, Sham and Egypt. His Sunan holds many hadith found in none of the other five. Later scholars counted it the sixth canonical book, though some preferred Malik's Muwatta in that place.

name: Al-Daraqutni
line: A Baghdad master who reviewed even the two Sahihs, chain by chain.
story: Named after the Dar al-Qutn quarter of Baghdad, he was famed for his memory and for uncovering hidden defects in narrations. His critique of about two hundred reports in the two Sahihs was answered point by point by later scholars, which only sharpened the science.
legacy: His Sunan and his book of defects ('Ilal) remain standard works of hadith criticism.

name: Al-Hakim al-Nishapuri
line: He gathered hadith he judged to meet al-Bukhari's and Muslim's standards but missing from their books.
story: Born in Nishapur, he served as a judge and studied with a great many teachers. His Mustadrak was later reviewed by al-Dhahabi, who found many of its gradings too lenient. He also wrote one of the first manuals on the sciences of hadith.
legacy: His manual shaped how later scholars taught the science of hadith.

name: Al-Bayhaqi
line: A scholar of Khurasan whose Great Sunan supports Shafi'i law with hadith.
story: A student of al-Hakim, he wrote al-Sunan al-Kubra and Dala'il al-Nubuwwah on the signs of prophethood. Al-Juwayni said every Shafi'i owes a debt to al-Shafi'i except al-Bayhaqi, to whom al-Shafi'i owes one.
legacy: His books remain standard references in Shafi'i fiqh and hadith.

name: Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi
line: His History of Baghdad records the lives of some 7,800 people of the city.
story: A preacher and hadith master, he wrote handbooks on how hadith should be taught, copied and checked. On Hajj he read Sahih al-Bukhari with Karima al-Marwaziyya in Makkah, in a matter of days.
legacy: Tarikh Baghdad became the model for the great city histories, such as Ibn Asakir's of Damascus.

name: Ibn Abd al-Barr
line: The great hadith scholar of the Muslim West, who explained the Muwatta in depth.
story: Born in Cordoba, he never travelled east yet became the West's leading authority. His al-Tamhid and al-Istidhkar explain the hadith of the Muwatta and the views of scholars, and al-Isti'ab gathers the lives of the Companions. He died at Xativa.
legacy: His works remain the deepest Maliki commentary on the Muwatta.

name: Ibn Hazm
line: A Cordoban minister turned scholar who wrote on law, religions and love.
story: After the fall of the Cordoban caliphate he left politics. He championed the Zahiri method, holding to the plain text and rejecting analogy, and wrote a landmark study of other religions. His Ring of the Dove is a gentle classic on love.
legacy: His study of religions is one of the first works of comparative religion.
note: His sharp tongue against other scholars was famous, and his Zahiri views remained a minority.

name: Qadi Iyad
line: A Maliki judge whose al-Shifa, on the Prophet ﷺ, is read worldwide.
story: He served as judge in Ceuta and Granada and wrote on hadith and the lives of Maliki scholars. Al-Shifa sets out the Prophet's ﷺ qualities and the love and respect owed to him. After resisting the Almohads, he died in Marrakesh.
legacy: Al-Shifa is still taught, recited and commented on from Morocco to Indonesia.

name: Ibn Asakir
line: His History of Damascus, in some eighty volumes, is one of the largest works of Islamic history.
story: He studied with well over a thousand teachers, about eighty of them women. Nur al-Din built a house of hadith for him in Damascus, where he taught. His history gathers the lives of everyone of note who lived in or passed through the city.
legacy: Tarikh Dimashq preserves countless reports found nowhere else.

name: Ibn al-Jawzi
line: A Hanbali preacher whose sermons in Baghdad drew vast crowds.
story: He wrote hundreds of books on history, hadith, tafsir and the soul, and exposed fabricated hadith in al-Mawdu'at. Exiled to Wasit for five years late in life, he returned to preach again. He is said to have saved the shavings of his reed pens to heat the water for his funeral washing.
legacy: His Sayd al-Khatir and books on fabricated hadith are still widely read.

name: Ibn Qudamah
line: A refugee from Crusader Palestine who wrote al-Mughni, a vast work of comparative law.
story: His family fled the Crusaders from Jamma'il near Nablus to Damascus when he was a boy. He is reported to have marched with Salah al-Din's army, and he wrote al-Mughni, setting out the views of all the schools on each question.
legacy: Al-Mughni is still a first reference for comparative fiqh.
note: His presence in Salah al-Din's campaigns is reported by his biographers.

name: Al-Izz ibn Abd al-Salam
line: A scholar who told the Mamluk emirs they were still legally slaves and must be sold for the treasury.
story: Expelled from Damascus for condemning its ruler's alliance with the Crusaders, he moved to Cairo. There he ruled that the Mamluk emirs, never formally freed, must be sold and freed, with the price going to the public. Before Ain Jalut he ruled that a war tax was allowed only after the emirs gave up their own gold.
legacy: His book on the aims of the law, Qawa'id al-Ahkam, prepared the way for later maqasid thought.
lesson: A scholar's duty is to speak the truth to those in power.

name: Al-Nawawi
line: Author of the Forty Hadith and Riyad al-Salihin, read in homes and mosques everywhere.
story: He came to Damascus from the village of Nawa at eighteen, attended up to twelve lessons a day, and lived simply, never marrying. He wrote a great commentary on Sahih Muslim and works that settled the Shafi'i school, and refused to approve a war tax Baybars wanted from the people. He died in his mid-forties.
legacy: Riyad al-Salihin and the Forty Hadith are among the most read Islamic books after the Quran.

name: Al-Dhahabi
line: A Damascus historian who wrote the lives of thousands of scholars and narrators.
story: Of Turkmen descent and the son of a goldsmith, he studied with hundreds of teachers, women among them. His Siyar A'lam al-Nubala and Tarikh al-Islam judge narrators with balanced care. He lost his sight in his last years.
legacy: His dictionaries of narrators are still the working tools of hadith study.

name: Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani
role: Commander of the faithful in hadith
line: Author of Fath al-Bari, the greatest commentary on Sahih al-Bukhari.
story: Orphaned in Cairo, he memorised the Quran by nine and studied in Egypt, the Hijaz and Yemen. He served as chief Shafi'i judge of Mamluk Egypt and spent some twenty-five years writing Fath al-Bari. He also wrote Bulugh al-Maram and huge dictionaries of narrators.
legacy: Fath al-Bari is the standard key to Sahih al-Bukhari.

name: Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli
line: A Cairo scholar who began the short and clear Tafsir al-Jalalayn.
story: Known for piety and for refusing a judgeship, he wrote a brief tafsir from Surah al-Kahf to the end, and al-Fatihah. Al-Suyuti finished the first half after his death, and the joint work was named after the two Jalals.
legacy: Tafsir al-Jalalayn is among the most studied tafsirs in the world.

name: Al-Suyuti
line: A Cairo scholar of hundreds of works, who finished Tafsir al-Jalalayn.
story: He wrote on tafsir, hadith, grammar, history and medicine, and believed himself the renewer of his century. He completed Tafsir al-Jalalayn begun by al-Mahalli and wrote al-Itqan on the sciences of the Quran. At forty he withdrew from public life to write.
legacy: Al-Itqan and al-Jalalayn are still first books for students of the Quran.

name: Ibn Abidin
line: His Radd al-Muhtar is the final reference of the Hanafi school for most muftis.
story: He trained first in Shafi'i law and then turned Hanafi. Radd al-Muhtar, his commentary on al-Durr al-Mukhtar, gathered centuries of Hanafi rulings into one work.
legacy: It became the standard reference of late Ottoman courts and of South Asian muftis.

name: Al-Shawkani
line: A Yemeni judge who urged Muslims to return directly to the Quran and hadith.
story: Raised in the Zaydi tradition of Yemen, he became chief judge of Sana'a and argued against blind following of any school. His Nayl al-Awtar on legal hadith and his tafsir Fath al-Qadir are widely used by Sunnis.
legacy: His call for ijtihad inspired many later reform movements.

name: Al-Tabari
line: His tafsir and his world history are the foundations of both fields.
story: From Amol near the Caspian, he left home at about twelve to study and settled in Baghdad. His Jami' al-Bayan gathers the early explanations of each verse with their chains, and his History of the Prophets and Kings runs from Creation to his own day. His own school of law did not last.
legacy: Almost every later tafsir and history draws on him.

name: Al-Baghawi
line: His clear tafsir and his Masabih al-Sunnah were standard texts for centuries.
story: From Bagh near Herat, he was called 'reviver of the Sunnah'. His tafsir, Ma'alim al-Tanzil, keeps to the sayings of the early generations and avoids weak reports. His Masabih al-Sunnah was later expanded into the much-loved Mishkat al-Masabih.

name: Al-Zamakhshari
line: A grammarian whose tafsir al-Kashshaf is prized for showing the Quran's eloquence.
story: Born in Zamakhshar in Khwarazm, he lived long in Makkah and was called 'Jar Allah', neighbour of God. Al-Kashshaf explains the Quran's language and rhetoric with rare skill.
legacy: Later commentators such as al-Baydawi kept his insights on language.
note: He was a Mu'tazili, and Sunni scholars read his tafsir with care; al-Baydawi and others kept its linguistic insights while dropping its Mu'tazili views.

name: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi
line: An Ash'ari theologian whose Great Tafsir answers philosophers and theologians verse by verse.
story: From Rayy, he debated across Khwarazm, Transoxiana and Herat, where Ghurid and Khwarazmian rulers honoured him. His tafsir, Mafatih al-Ghayb, brings theology, philosophy and natural science into the reading of the Quran.
legacy: Ash'ari theologians built on his work for centuries.
note: Not to be confused with the physician Abu Bakr al-Razi.

name: Al-Qurtubi
line: An Andalusian scholar whose tafsir draws the laws out of every verse.
story: Born in Cordoba, he left after the city fell to Castile in 1236 and settled in Upper Egypt. His al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran discusses the rulings in each verse and the views of the schools. He also wrote al-Tadhkirah on death and the Hereafter.
legacy: His tafsir is the main reference for the legal verses of the Quran.

name: Ibn Kathir
line: His tafsir, explaining the Quran by the Quran and hadith, is the most read in the world.
story: Born near Busra in Syria, he studied in Damascus under Ibn Taymiyyah and the hadith master al-Mizzi, whose daughter he married. His tafsir explains verses first by other verses, then by hadith and the words of the Companions, and flags Isra'iliyyat. He also wrote al-Bidayah wa al-Nihayah, a history from Creation to the end of time.
legacy: Abridged and translated into many languages, it is often a reader's first tafsir.

name: Rabi'ah al-Adawiyyah
line: A freed slave of Basra who taught that God should be worshipped out of love alone.
story: Tradition says she was sold into slavery as a child and freed because of her devotion. She lived in poverty, turned down marriage and wealth, and is remembered for prayers of love for God, not fear of Hell or hope of Paradise alone.
legacy: Her love-centred devotion became a lasting theme of Sufi poetry.
note: Most stories about her come from later writers such as Attar and are hard to verify; her dates are traditional.

name: Al-Junayd al-Baghdadi
line: Called 'master of the group', he tied the spiritual path firmly to the Quran and Sunnah.
story: Trained in fiqh and taught the inner path by his uncle Sari al-Saqati, he favoured sober self-control over ecstatic outbursts. He said: 'This knowledge of ours is bound to the Quran and the Sunnah.'
legacy: Most Sufi orders trace their chains through him.

name: Abu Mansur al-Maturidi
line: A Hanafi theologian whose creed became the school of most Hanafis.
story: Working in Samarkand under the Samanids, far from Baghdad, he defended Sunni belief against the Mu'tazilis and others. His Kitab al-Tawhid and his tafsir Ta'wilat al-Quran survive. His school differs from al-Ash'ari's on only a few points.
legacy: The Ottomans, Mughals and Central Asian Muslims followed his theology.

name: Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari
line: A Mu'tazili who turned to defend the creed of Ahmad ibn Hanbal with reasoned argument.
story: A student of the Mu'tazili al-Jubba'i for decades, he publicly renounced their teaching around the age of forty in the mosque of Basra. He then used their own tools of argument to defend Sunni belief: that the Quran is God's uncreated speech and that believers will see Him in the Hereafter.
legacy: The Ash'ari school became the theology of most Shafi'i and Maliki scholars.

name: Al-Mawardi
line: His Ordinances of Government was the first full Muslim treatise on the state.
story: A Shafi'i judge, he served as an envoy between the Abbasid caliph and the Buyid and Seljuk rulers. Al-Ahkam al-Sultaniyyah sets out the duties of caliph, ministers, judges and governors. He also wrote Adab al-Dunya wa al-Din on ethics.
legacy: His book became the classic Sunni text on political authority.

name: Al-Qushayri
line: His Risalah set out the Sufi path in the language of Sunni law and creed.
story: A Shafi'i and Ash'ari scholar of Nishapur, he wrote al-Risalah al-Qushayriyyah to show that true Sufism agrees with the Sharia, and warned against those who used it as an excuse for laxity. He also wrote a Sufi tafsir, Lata'if al-Isharat.
legacy: The Risalah became the standard textbook of Sufism.

name: Al-Juwayni
line: Al-Ghazali's teacher, who taught in Makkah and Madinah during a years-long exile.
story: Forced out of Khurasan for some years, he taught in Makkah and Madinah, earning the title Imam al-Haramayn. Nizam al-Mulk then built the Nizamiyya of Nishapur for him. He wrote major works in Shafi'i law, legal theory and Ash'ari theology.
legacy: His students, led by al-Ghazali, carried his methods across the Muslim world.

name: Al-Ghazali
line: A famous professor who left everything to seek certainty, then wrote the Revival of the Religious Sciences.
story: Head of the Nizamiyya in Baghdad by his mid-thirties, he fell into a crisis of doubt and lost his voice. In 1095 he left and spent years in seclusion in Damascus, Jerusalem and on Hajj. His Ihya brought law, theology and the inner life together, and his Incoherence of the Philosophers challenged Ibn Sina.
legacy: The Ihya remains a guide for the heart across the Muslim world.
lesson: Learning is worth little if it does not reform the heart.

name: Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani
line: A Hanbali preacher of Baghdad whose followers formed the first widespread Sufi order.
story: He came to Baghdad at eighteen, studied Hanbali law, and became a preacher whose sermons moved great crowds to repentance. His school trained students from many lands, and his talks are collected in al-Fath al-Rabbani.
legacy: The Qadiriyya spread from Iraq to Africa, India and Southeast Asia.
note: Most accounts place his birth in Gilan in Persia; some say Jil near Baghdad. Many miracle stories about him are later legend.

name: Ibn Arabi
line: A mystic from Murcia whose writings shaped later Sufi thought and drew sharp criticism.
story: He travelled from al-Andalus through North Africa to Makkah, where he began al-Futuhat al-Makkiyyah, and settled in Damascus. His ideas, later summed up as 'unity of being', were embraced by many Sufis and condemned by scholars such as Ibn Taymiyyah.
legacy: His vocabulary runs through much later Sufi poetry in Persian, Turkish and Malay.
note: Opinions range from 'greatest master' to heretic; many defenders say his words are misread when taken literally.

name: Rumi
line: A jurist of Konya whose meeting with a wandering dervish made him the poet of the Masnavi.
story: His family fled the Mongol advance from Khurasan to Anatolia, where he taught law and preached like his father. In 1244 he met Shams of Tabriz and turned to poetry. His Masnavi, some 25,000 verses in Persian, retells Quranic stories and hadith as lessons for the soul.
legacy: The Mevlevi order of whirling dervishes grew from his circle, and he is among the most read poets in the world.
note: His birthplace is given as Balkh or Vakhsh in today's Tajikistan.

name: Sa'di
line: A Persian poet whose Gulistan and Bustan taught manners to centuries of schoolchildren.
story: He left Shiraz as the Mongols threatened, studied at the Nizamiyya of Baghdad and spent decades travelling. Back home he wrote the Bustan and the Gulistan, stories and verses on justice, humility and kindness. His lines on all people being limbs of one body are known across the world.
legacy: The Gulistan was a first reader in Persian from Istanbul to Delhi.

name: Ibn Taymiyyah
line: A Damascus scholar who resisted the Mongols in word and battle and died in prison.
story: His family fled Harran from the Mongols when he was a boy. He urged resistance to the Ilkhanid invasions and rode with the Mamluk army at Shaqhab in 1303. His sharp positions on creed and practice brought him repeated jailings, and he died in the citadel of Damascus.
legacy: His writings on belief and law, revived by later reformers, are among the most influential of recent centuries.
note: He remains debated: admirers call him Shaykh al-Islam, while many Ash'aris and Sufis rejected some of his views.

name: Ibn al-Qayyim
line: Ibn Taymiyyah's closest student, who wrote warmly on the heart and the Prophet's ﷺ way.
story: Son of the caretaker (qayyim) of the Jawziyyah school in Damascus, he stayed with his teacher through imprisonment. His books include Zad al-Ma'ad on the Prophet's ﷺ guidance, Madarij al-Salikin on the stations of the soul, and a work on Prophetic medicine.
legacy: His books on the heart are among the most read classical works today.

name: Baha al-Din Naqshband
line: A master of Bukhara whose quiet path, 'the heart with God, the hands at work', spread across Asia.
story: He taught silent remembrance of God in the heart, kept up amid daily work, rather than withdrawal from the world. His order spread through Central Asia, India, the Ottoman lands and China.
legacy: Naqshbandi masters, Ahmad Sirhindi among them, later shaped religious life in the Mughal and Ottoman empires.

name: Mu'in al-Din Chishti
line: A Sufi from Sistan whose shrine at Ajmer is one of the most visited in South Asia.
story: After years of travel through Khurasan and Iraq, he settled in Ajmer around the time of the Ghurid conquest of northern India. He taught generosity and service to the poor, and many local people embraced Islam through his circle.
legacy: The Chishti order became the most widespread Sufi path in South Asia.
note: Most details of his life come from later hagiography.

name: Nizam al-Din Awliya
line: A Delhi Sufi whose open kitchen fed thousands and who kept away from the sultans' courts.
story: He refused to attend the courts of the Delhi sultans; his lodge is said to have had two doors, and if a king came in by one he would leave by the other. Rich and poor ate together at his kitchen, and the poet Amir Khusrau was his devoted disciple.
legacy: His shrine in Delhi is still alive with prayer and qawwali every evening.
note: The sayings attributed to him come from his disciples' records and later tradition.

name: Ahmad Sirhindi
line: A Naqshbandi scholar who called the Mughal elite back to the Sharia after Akbar's experiments.
story: When the emperor Akbar promoted a court cult blending faiths, Sirhindi insisted on the Sharia and the Sunnah through hundreds of letters to nobles. Jahangir jailed him for about a year at Gwalior, then released and honoured him.
legacy: His followers called him Mujaddid Alf Thani; his Mujaddidi branch of the Naqshbandiyya spread from India to the Ottoman lands.

name: Abdullah ibn Alawi al-Haddad
line: A blind scholar of Tarim whose short litany is recited from Yemen to Indonesia.
story: He lost his sight to smallpox as a small child but memorised the Quran and became the leading scholar of Hadramawt. He wrote short, clear books on faith and character, and composed the Ratib al-Haddad, a litany of verses and remembrance.
legacy: Hadrami traders and scholars carried his books and litany around the Indian Ocean, to East Africa and Southeast Asia.

name: Shah Waliullah
line: A Delhi scholar who translated the Quran into Persian so ordinary readers could understand it.
story: He grew up as the Mughal state was breaking apart after Aurangzeb. After studying hadith in Makkah and Madinah, he taught in Delhi, translated the Quran into Persian, and wrote Hujjat Allah al-Balighah on the wisdom behind the Sharia.
legacy: His sons translated the Quran into Urdu, and most later South Asian movements, Deoband among them, claim his heritage.

name: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab
line: A Najdi scholar whose call to strict tawhid, allied with the house of Saud, reshaped Arabia.
story: Born in al-Uyaynah and trained in Najd, Madinah and Basra, he preached against the veneration of tombs and saints that he saw around him. In 1744 he allied with Muhammad ibn Saud of Diriyah, a pact that underlies the Saudi state. His Kitab al-Tawhid is his best-known book.
legacy: His teachings remain the official religious school of Saudi Arabia.
note: Views of him differ sharply: followers see a revival of pure tawhid, while many scholars of his day and later criticised his movement's harshness toward other Muslims.

name: Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad
line: A Basran from Oman who wrote the first Arabic dictionary and mapped the metres of Arabic poetry.
story: He arranged Kitab al-Ayn by the sounds of the letters, from the throat to the lips, and worked out the metres of Arabic verse. He also replaced the old coloured dots with the vowel marks still used in the Quran today: fatha, damma and kasra.
legacy: Every mushaf printed today carries his vowel signs.
note: His death is given between 170 and 175 AH.

name: Sibawayh
line: A young Persian whose 'al-Kitab' became the foundation of Arabic grammar.
story: He came to Basra to study hadith and, after being corrected for a mistake in Arabic, resolved to master the language. Trained by al-Khalil, he wrote al-Kitab, the first full description of Arabic grammar. After losing a famous debate in Baghdad, he went home to Persia and died young.
legacy: Grammarians have called his work simply 'the Book' for twelve centuries.
note: His birth and death years are uncertain; he died in his thirties or early forties.

name: Ibn Muqla
line: An Abbasid vizier who set the proportions of Arabic script that calligraphers still follow.
story: He measured each letter by the rhombic dot of the pen and the height of the alif, giving the cursive scripts their balanced form. Three times vizier, he fell in court intrigues and lost his right hand, yet he is said to have kept writing with a pen tied to his arm.
legacy: The six classical scripts used to copy the Quran rest on his system.

name: Mahmud al-Kashgari
line: A Turkic scholar of Kashgar who wrote the first dictionary of Turkic languages, in Arabic.
story: Writing in Baghdad in the 1070s, he compiled Diwan Lughat al-Turk to teach Arabic-speakers the language of the Turks, who now ruled much of the Muslim world. The book includes a round map of the known world with the Turkic lands at its centre.
legacy: It is the oldest major record of the Turkic languages.
note: His birth and death dates are estimates.

name: Ibn Malik
line: An Andalusian grammarian whose thousand-line poem on grammar is still memorised.
story: He left Jaen in al-Andalus for the east and taught in Aleppo and Damascus. His Alfiyyah puts the whole of Arabic grammar into about a thousand rhyming lines, and generations of students have learned it by heart.
legacy: The Alfiyyah and its commentaries are core texts of traditional madrasas.

name: Ibn Manzur
line: A judge whose Lisan al-Arab is the best-known classical Arabic dictionary.
story: He served as a judge in Tripoli in North Africa and as a clerk in the Mamluk chancery in Cairo. Lisan al-Arab gathers the great dictionaries before it, with examples from the Quran, hadith and poetry, into one huge work.
legacy: Translators and students of the Quran still turn to it for the meaning of words.

name: Ibn Ajurrum
role: Author of the first grammar primer
line: A Fez grammarian whose short Ajurrumiyyah is often the first grammar book a student reads.
story: Of Berber origin, he taught Quran recitation and grammar in Fez. His Muqaddimah, known as the Ajurrumiyyah, compresses Arabic grammar into a few pages.
legacy: From West Africa to Indonesia, children begin Arabic grammar with his primer.

name: Asim ibn Abi al-Najud
line: The Kufan reader whose reading, through his student Hafs, is the one most Muslims recite today.
story: He learned the Quran from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, who had learned it from Uthman, Ali, Ibn Masud and Zayd ibn Thabit. He was famed for his beautiful voice and precise Arabic, and two students carried his reading: Hafs and Shu'bah.
legacy: Hafs from Asim is the reading of most printed mushafs.
note: His death is given as 127 or 128 AH.

name: Hafs ibn Sulayman
line: Asim's stepson, whose transmission is the reading in most printed Qurans.
story: Raised in Asim's house, he learned the Quran from him letter by letter and later taught in Baghdad and Makkah. The Cairo edition of 1924, printed in his reading, made it the global standard.
legacy: Most of the world's Muslims recite the Quran as Hafs passed it on.
note: Hadith critics rated him weak as a hadith narrator, but he is the authority in recitation.

name: Nafi' al-Madani
line: The Quran reader of Madinah whose reading, through Warsh and Qalun, is recited across Africa.
story: He learned the Quran from some seventy tabi'un and led the readers of the Prophet's ﷺ Mosque for decades. Malik called his reading the Sunnah. His students Warsh and Qalun carried it to Egypt and beyond.
legacy: The Warsh and Qalun readings of North and West Africa come from him.
note: Not the same person as Nafi', the freedman of Ibn Umar.

name: Warsh
line: An Egyptian reader whose transmission of Nafi' is recited across North and West Africa.
story: Born in Egypt, he travelled to Madinah and read the whole Quran with Nafi' several times. Back in Egypt he led the Quran readers for decades.
legacy: Warsh is the main reading of the Maghreb and much of West Africa.

name: Al-Qasim al-Shatibi
line: A blind Andalusian whose poem al-Shatibiyyah is how students still learn the seven readings.
story: From Xativa in al-Andalus, he settled in Cairo, where Salah al-Din's chief minister al-Qadi al-Fadil made him head of his school. His poem Hirz al-Amani, known as al-Shatibiyyah, sets out the seven readings in about 1,170 lines.
legacy: Reciters who master the seven readings still memorise his poem.
note: Not the same person as Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi, the Granada jurist.

name: Ibn al-Jazari
line: A Damascus scholar who confirmed the ten readings and set down the rules of tajwid.
story: He travelled through Egypt and Anatolia, and after Timur's victory at Ankara he was taken to Samarkand. He later served as judge in Shiraz. His al-Nashr fi al-Qira'at al-Ashr established the ten readings, and his short poem al-Jazariyyah is the basic text of tajwid.
legacy: Tajwid teachers worldwide still begin with al-Jazariyyah.

name: Jabir ibn Hayyan
line: The name behind a huge body of early Arabic chemistry, much of it written by later hands.
story: Tradition places him in Kufa in the 8th century as a student of Ja'far al-Sadiq. Works under his name describe distillation, crystallisation and new substances, and their Latin translations shaped European chemistry.
legacy: Words such as alkali and alembic reached Europe through this tradition.
note: Historians think most of the Jabirian writings came from a circle of later authors in the 9th-10th centuries, and even his existence is debated.

name: Al-Khwarizmi
line: A scholar of the House of Wisdom whose book gave the world 'algebra' and whose name gave 'algorithm'.
story: His family came from Khwarazm in Central Asia. In Baghdad under al-Mamun he wrote a book on al-jabr wa al-muqabalah, solving equations for trade, land measurement and the Quran's rules of inheritance. His book on Indian numerals carried the decimal system to Europe.
legacy: Algebra and the 'Arabic' numerals used worldwide spread from his books.

name: Al-Kindi
line: The first great philosopher writing in Arabic, who also pioneered code-breaking.
story: An Arab of the tribe of Kinda, born in Kufa, he worked among the translators of Baghdad under al-Mamun and his successors. He argued that philosophy and revelation agree, and wrote the earliest known work on breaking codes by counting how often letters appear.
legacy: Frequency analysis, his method, is still the starting point of cryptography.

name: Banu Musa
role: Engineers of the House of Wisdom
line: Three brothers of Baghdad who wrote the Book of Ingenious Devices.
story: Muhammad, Ahmad and al-Hasan, sons of Musa ibn Shakir, were raised under al-Mamun's care. They paid for translations of Greek science and wrote on geometry and astronomy. Their Kitab al-Hiyal, around 850, describes about a hundred devices, many driven by water and air pressure.
legacy: Their automatic valves and controls were early steps toward mechanical engineering.
note: This entry stands for all three brothers.

name: Abbas ibn Firnas
line: An Andalusian inventor said to have flown with wings of feathers on a wooden frame.
story: A poet, musician and astronomer at the Umayyad court of Cordoba, he is credited with cutting rock crystal and building a model of the heavens. A later historian reports that he glided some distance with a winged suit, landed hard, and regretted not giving himself a tail.
note: The flight is known from al-Maqqari, writing in the 17th century and citing an earlier poem.

name: Al-Battani
line: An astronomer whose measured year and star tables were cited by Copernicus.
story: Working at Raqqa on the Euphrates, he measured the solar year as 365 days, 5 hours, 46 minutes and 24 seconds, and made trigonometry a working tool of astronomy. Copernicus quoted him many times.
legacy: His tables were used in Europe for centuries.
note: He came from a Sabian family of Harran but was himself Muslim.

name: Abu Bakr al-Razi
line: A physician who first told smallpox from measles and ran the hospitals of Rayy and Baghdad.
story: It is said that he chose the site of a Baghdad hospital by hanging meat in different districts and seeing where it rotted slowest. His al-Hawi gathered all the medicine he knew with his own case notes, and his treatise on smallpox and measles was used in Europe for centuries.
legacy: His clinical notes are an early model of the medical case record.
note: His death is given as 925 or 935. His philosophical views on prophecy were rejected by Muslim scholars, while his medicine was widely respected.

name: Al-Farabi
line: A philosopher from Central Asia, called the 'Second Teacher' after Aristotle.
story: Born near Farab on the Syr Darya, he worked in Baghdad and died in Damascus under the Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla. He wrote on logic, music and the ideal state in The Virtuous City. Ibn Sina said he understood Aristotle's Metaphysics only after reading al-Farabi.
legacy: His Great Book of Music was a classic of music theory.
note: Some of his philosophical positions were later criticised by al-Ghazali.

name: Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi
line: An astronomer whose Book of Fixed Stars has the first known record of the Andromeda galaxy.
story: Working at the Buyid court, he checked Ptolemy's star catalogue by his own observation and recorded the Arabic star names. His Book of Fixed Stars (964) describes a 'little cloud' that is the Andromeda galaxy.
legacy: Many star names used today, such as Aldebaran and Altair, came to Europe through his tradition.

name: Al-Zahrawi
line: A surgeon of Cordoba whose illustrated book of instruments taught Europe surgery for centuries.
story: Court physician to the caliphs of Cordoba, he wrote al-Tasrif, a medical encyclopedia in thirty parts. Its last part, on surgery, shows some two hundred instruments, many of his own design, and was translated into Latin.
legacy: Surgeons in Europe used his book until the Renaissance.

name: Ibn al-Haytham
line: A scholar of Basra and Cairo who showed that we see by light entering the eye.
story: Later biographers say he feigned madness to escape a task from the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, regulating the Nile, and used his confinement to study light. His Book of Optics tested ideas by experiment, using a dark room with a pinhole: the camera obscura.
legacy: Latin translations shaped Roger Bacon, Kepler and the experimental method.
note: The madness story is reported by later biographers.

name: Al-Biruni
role: Scholar of India and the stars
line: A Khwarazmian polymath who measured the earth and wrote the first deep study of India.
story: Brought to Ghazna by Mahmud of Ghazna, he went with the sultan's campaigns into India, learned Sanskrit, and wrote a fair-minded account of Hindu beliefs and science. Using a mountain near Nandana, he estimated the earth's radius remarkably well.
legacy: His book on India is still read as a model of studying another culture with fairness.

name: Ibn Sina
line: A physician-philosopher whose Canon of Medicine was taught in Europe for centuries.
story: Born near Bukhara, he had memorised the Quran by ten and was a court physician in his teens. Moving between courts, he wrote the Canon of Medicine and the Book of Healing, a vast work of philosophy. He died at Hamadan, where his tomb stands.
legacy: The Canon was a standard medical textbook in Europe into the 17th century.
note: Al-Ghazali criticised some of his philosophical views, such as the eternity of the world.

name: Omar Khayyam
line: A mathematician who reformed the Persian calendar and solved cubic equations, later famed for poetry.
story: Working for the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah, he led the team that made the Jalali calendar, more accurate than the Julian. He solved cubic equations using conic sections. Quatrains attributed to him became world-famous through an English translation.
legacy: The Iranian calendar still follows the system his team designed.
note: How many of the quatrains are really his is uncertain, and their doubting tone may not reflect his own beliefs.

name: Al-Idrisi
line: A geographer who made a great world map for the Norman king of Sicily.
story: Born in Ceuta to a family descended from the Idrisid rulers, he studied in Cordoba and travelled widely. Roger II invited him to Palermo, where his Book of Roger (1154) and a silver world map combined travellers' reports into the best geography of the age.
legacy: His maps were copied in both Muslim and Christian lands for centuries.

name: Ibn Rushd
line: A Maliki judge of Cordoba whose commentaries on Aristotle made him 'the Commentator' in Europe.
story: Grandson of a chief judge of Cordoba, he served as judge in Seville and Cordoba and as physician to the Almohad caliph. He wrote Bidayat al-Mujtahid, a classic of comparative fiqh, and The Incoherence of the Incoherence in reply to al-Ghazali. Late in life he was briefly exiled and his books burned, then restored to favour.
legacy: Latin translations of his commentaries shaped European philosophy for centuries.

name: Al-Jazari
line: An engineer whose book of machines includes the famous elephant clock.
story: Chief engineer to the Artuqid princes of Diyarbakir, he described some fifty machines in his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices (1206). They include water pumps with crankshafts, automata and the elephant clock.
legacy: His crank-and-rod mechanisms prefigure parts of later engines.

name: Ibn al-Baytar
line: A botanist from Malaga whose book of simple medicines listed some 1,400 plants and drugs.
story: He collected plants across North Africa, Anatolia and Syria and served the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil as chief herbalist in Cairo. His great compendium of simple drugs joins Greek knowledge with his own field observations.
legacy: His work was a standard pharmacy reference in the Muslim world for centuries.

name: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi
line: An astronomer who built the Maragha observatory under the Mongols and saved many books.
story: Held for years at the Ismaili fortress of Alamut, he joined Hulagu after its fall. He persuaded the khan to fund an observatory at Maragha in 1259, whose library gathered books from ravaged cities. His 'Tusi couple' reappears in the work of Copernicus.
legacy: Maragha trained a school of astronomers whose models led toward modern astronomy.
note: He was a Twelver Shia theologian. Accounts that he urged Hulagu on at Baghdad are disputed.

name: Ibn al-Nafis
line: A Cairo physician who first described how blood passes through the lungs.
story: Trained in Damascus, he worked in Cairo's great hospitals. In a commentary on Ibn Sina's Canon he corrected Galen and described the pulmonary circulation, three centuries before European writers. He left his house and books to the Mansuri hospital.
legacy: His discovery is a milestone in the history of physiology.

name: Ibn al-Shatir
line: The timekeeper of Damascus's great mosque, whose planetary models match those of Copernicus.
story: As muwaqqit he set the prayer times and built a great sundial for a minaret of the Umayyad Mosque. His planetary models, free of Ptolemy's equant, are mathematically the same as those Copernicus used about 150 years later.
legacy: A copy of his sundial still marks the prayer times in the mosque.

name: Jamshid al-Kashi
line: Ulugh Beg's mathematician, who calculated pi to sixteen decimal places.
story: From Kashan in Persia, he joined Ulugh Beg's observatory and wrote The Key of Arithmetic. In 1424 he computed pi correctly to sixteen decimal places, a record that stood for almost two centuries.
legacy: His decimal fractions and methods were used by astronomers for generations.

name: Taqi al-Din
line: Chief astronomer of the Ottomans, who built an observatory in Istanbul and wrote on mechanical clocks.
story: Born in Damascus, he worked in Cairo and Istanbul, writing on clocks, optics and astronomy. In 1577 Sultan Murad III built him an observatory at Tophane. After a comet that year was blamed for misfortunes, the observatory was torn down in 1580.
legacy: His clock treatise is among the earliest on spring-driven clocks in the Muslim world.

name: Piri Reis
line: An Ottoman admiral whose 1513 world map preserves a lost map of the Americas.
story: Nephew of the corsair Kemal Reis, he sailed the Mediterranean for years. His 1513 map, drawn from some twenty sources including one by Columbus, shows the coasts of South America and Africa. His Kitab-i Bahriye is a detailed guide to Mediterranean sailing. He was executed in Cairo in old age after a failed campaign.
legacy: His map is one of the oldest surviving to show the Americas.

name: Mimar Sinan
line: The chief architect of three sultans, who built the Suleymaniye and the Selimiye mosques.
story: Taken as a Christian boy from Anatolia in the devshirme, he became a Janissary engineer before being named chief architect in 1539. Over some fifty years he and his office designed hundreds of buildings: mosques, bridges, schools and baths. He called the Selimiye in Edirne his masterwork.
legacy: His pupil Sedefkar Mehmed Agha built the Blue Mosque, and his style shaped cities from Bosnia to Egypt.

name: Ustad Ahmad Lahori
line: The architect traditionally credited with designing the Taj Mahal.
story: Working for Shah Jahan, he is named by his son's writings as the designer of the Taj Mahal in Agra and the Red Fort in Delhi. The Taj's great gate carries Surah al-Fajr's call to the soul at rest to enter Paradise.
legacy: The Taj became the emblem of Mughal architecture.
note: The attribution rests on later family sources; the building was the work of many masters.

name: Sayyida Nafisa
line: A descendant of the Prophet ﷺ whose home in Cairo was a centre of learning, visited by al-Shafi'i.
story: A great-granddaughter of Hasan ibn Ali, she memorised the Quran young, studied in Madinah and settled in Egypt. Al-Shafi'i attended her gatherings and asked for her prayers, and when he died his bier was brought to her house so she could pray over him.
legacy: Her shrine and mosque in Cairo remain among the city's most loved.

name: Fatima al-Fihri
line: A merchant's daughter who used her inheritance to found the Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez in 859.
story: Her family came to Fez from Kairouan. With the wealth her father left her, she built a mosque for her community and is said to have fasted every day until it was finished. Al-Qarawiyyin grew into a centre of learning that still teaches today.
legacy: Al-Qarawiyyin is often called the oldest existing university in the world.
note: Her story comes mainly from the 14th-century chronicler Ibn Abi Zar, and some historians question its details.

name: Al-Ijliyyah
line: A woman astrolabe maker of Aleppo, at the court of Sayf al-Dawla.
story: Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist names al-Ijliyyah, daughter of an astrolabe maker, among the instrument makers of her day, working for the Hamdanid ruler of Aleppo. Astrolabes were used to tell the time of prayer and find the direction of the qiblah.
note: All we know is one line in the Fihrist; the first name 'Mariam' is a modern addition.

name: Sutayta al-Mahamali
line: A Baghdad scholar praised for her skill in the arithmetic of inheritance and in law.
story: Daughter of the judge al-Husayn al-Mahamili, she studied Arabic, hadith and fiqh. Her biographers say she was expert in fara'id, the calculation of the Quran's inheritance shares, and gave fatwas alongside the jurists.
note: Modern claims that she solved particular equations go beyond the sources, which only praise her learning.

name: Karima al-Marwaziyya
line: A woman from Merv whose copy of Sahih al-Bukhari, taught in Makkah, became a standard text.
story: She heard the Sahih from al-Kushmihani, a student of al-Bukhari's student al-Firabri. Living in Makkah, she taught it to scholars from across the Muslim world, including al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, and made them check their copies against hers. She never married.
legacy: Her transmission is one of the main lines through which Sahih al-Bukhari reached later centuries.

name: Shuhda al-Katibah
line: A Baghdad calligrapher and hadith teacher known as 'the pride of women'.
story: Daughter of a scholar, she heard hadith from leading masters as a girl and lived long enough to become a sought-after link to them. Her fine handwriting earned her the name al-Katibah, the writer, and students crowded to her lessons.
note: Her full name is Shuhda bint Ahmad al-Ibari; her birth year is uncertain.

name: Fatima al-Samarqandi
line: A Hanafi jurist whose signature appeared on fatwas beside her father's and husband's.
story: Daughter of Ala al-Din al-Samarqandi, author of Tuhfat al-Fuqaha, she knew his book by heart. Her husband al-Kasani wrote a celebrated commentary on it, accepted as her dowry, and she corrected him when he erred. In Aleppo, under Nur al-Din, she taught and gave fatwas.
legacy: Her household produced one of the great books of Hanafi law, Bada'i al-Sana'i.
note: Her exact dates are not known.

name: Zaynab bint al-Kamal
line: A Damascus teacher who held licences from hundreds of scholars and taught for most of her ninety years.
story: Her family enrolled her for teaching licences as a small child, so she carried authority from scholars long dead by the time she taught. She never married, and students filled her lessons, reading whole books with her.
legacy: Her name appears in the chains of many later hadith scholars.
note: Ibn Battuta lists a Zaynab bint al-Kamal among the teachers who licensed him in Damascus in 1326.

name: A'ishah al-Ba'uniyyah
line: A Damascene poet and Sufi, the most prolific woman author in Arabic before modern times.
story: From a family of scholars, she memorised the Quran by eight, studied in Damascus and Cairo, and was licensed to teach and give fatwas. She wrote more than a dozen works, including long poems in praise of the Prophet ﷺ.

name: Ibn Ishaq
role: First biographer of the Prophet ﷺ
line: The first to write a full life of the Prophet ﷺ.
story: A Madinan student of al-Zuhri, he gathered reports on the Prophet's ﷺ life and campaigns and moved to Iraq, where he wrote for the Abbasid court. His original book is lost; it survives mainly in Ibn Hisham's edition and in quotations by al-Tabari.
legacy: Every later seerah stands on his work.
note: Hadith critics accepted him for the seerah but were cautious with his reports on law.

name: Al-Waqidi
line: A Madinan historian whose Kitab al-Maghazi details the Prophet's ﷺ campaigns.
story: He walked the battlefields and spoke with the children of the fighters to fix places and dates. Al-Mamun made him a judge in Baghdad. His secretary Ibn Sa'd built on his work.
note: Hadith critics rated him weak in hadith, while historians rely on his detail.

name: Ibn Hisham
line: He edited Ibn Ishaq's life of the Prophet ﷺ into the Sirah read today.
story: A grammarian of Basran family living in Egypt, he received Ibn Ishaq's work through its transmitter al-Bakka'i. He trimmed it, removing poems and stories he judged unsound or off the subject, and added notes on language.
legacy: Al-Sirah al-Nabawiyyah of Ibn Hisham is the classic seerah.

name: Ibn Sa'd
line: Al-Waqidi's secretary, whose Great Generations records the lives of the Companions and their students.
story: His Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir gives biographies of the Prophet ﷺ, the Companions, men and women, and the generations after them, region by region. Its volume on women is a key source on early Muslim women.
legacy: It became the model for the biographical dictionaries of Islamic learning.

name: Al-Baladhuri
line: His Conquest of the Lands tells how each region came under Muslim rule.
story: A courtier of the Abbasid caliphs, he gathered accounts of the conquests from Arabia to Sindh, region by region. He also wrote Ansab al-Ashraf on the genealogies and deeds of the Arab nobility.

name: Al-Mas'udi
line: A traveller called 'the Herodotus of the Arabs' for his Meadows of Gold.
story: Born in Baghdad, he journeyed to India, the East African coast, the Caspian and Syria, and settled in Egypt. His Muruj al-Dhahab is a world history full of geography, peoples and customs, and describes the monsoon trade of the Indian Ocean.

name: Ibn Fadlan
line: An Abbasid envoy whose report on the Volga Bulgars and the Rus is unique.
story: In 921 the caliph al-Muqtadir sent him with an embassy to the king of the Volga Bulgars, who had asked for teachers of Islam and help building a fort. His account describes the Turks, the Bulgars and the Rus, including a Rus ship burial.
legacy: The Volga Bulgars' Islam is the root of the faith of today's Tatars.

name: Al-Muqaddasi
line: A Jerusalem-born geographer who based his book on what he saw himself.
story: He spent some twenty years travelling across the Muslim world. His Best Divisions for Knowledge of the Regions describes cities, markets, weights, foods and dialects, and speaks with love of Jerusalem, his home.
legacy: His book is a founding work of human geography.

name: Ibn Jubayr
line: A secretary of Granada whose Hajj diary is a vivid picture of the Crusader-era world.
story: Setting out in 1183, he described Salah al-Din's Egypt, Makkah and Madinah, Baghdad, the Crusader ports of the Levant, and Norman Sicily on the way home. He died in Alexandria on a later journey.
legacy: His Rihla began the genre that Ibn Battuta later made famous.

name: Yaqut al-Hamawi
role: Author of the dictionary of places
line: A freed slave of Greek birth who wrote the great dictionary of places.
story: Born in Byzantine lands and sold as a boy in Baghdad, he was freed and worked as a travelling book dealer. His Mu'jam al-Buldan lists the towns and regions of the known world. He fled Merv as the Mongols approached, and died in Aleppo.
legacy: His dictionary preserves cities and libraries the Mongols destroyed.

name: Ibn al-Athir
role: Historian of the Crusades and Mongols
line: A Mosul historian whose Complete History runs from Creation to the Mongol invasions.
story: Al-Kamil fi al-Tarikh follows al-Tabari and continues to 1231, covering the Crusades and Salah al-Din. He wrote of the Mongol invasion as the greatest disaster ever to strike Islam, wishing his mother had not borne him to see it.
legacy: His history is a main Muslim source for the Crusades.

name: Ibn Battuta
line: A judge from Tangier who travelled some 117,000 km across the Muslim world and beyond.
story: He left for Hajj at twenty-one and did not return home for twenty-four years, travelling from Morocco to China and from the Volga to East Africa, and serving as judge in Delhi and the Maldives. In 1352 he crossed the Sahara to the Mali Empire. He dictated his Rihla to Ibn Juzayy in Fez.
legacy: His Rihla is a unique portrait of the 14th-century Muslim world.

name: Ibn Khaldun
line: A Tunisian scholar whose Muqaddimah explained how dynasties rise and fall.
story: He served courts across the Maghreb and al-Andalus, then wrote the Muqaddimah in a fortress in Algeria in 1377. It argues that group solidarity ('asabiyyah') builds states and luxury dissolves them. As a Maliki judge of Cairo, he met Timur outside Damascus in 1401.
legacy: He is counted among the founders of sociology and the philosophy of history.

name: Al-Maqrizi
line: A Cairo historian whose Khitat describes the city's streets, mosques and past.
story: A student of Ibn Khaldun, he served as market inspector of Cairo and wrote histories of Egypt's dynasties. In a short study of famines he blamed debased coinage and corruption for soaring prices.
legacy: His Khitat is still the guide to medieval Cairo.

name: Zheng He
line: A Muslim admiral of Ming China who led seven great fleets across the Indian Ocean to Africa.
story: Born Ma He to a Hui Muslim family in Yunnan whose father had made the Hajj, he was captured as a boy and rose at the Ming court. Between 1405 and 1433 his treasure fleets reached Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, and members of his crews visited Makkah.
legacy: Mosques in Indonesia and Malaysia honour him as part of the region's Muslim story.
note: He was an admiral and envoy, not a religious scholar. His death is given as 1433 or 1435, and his own Hajj is not confirmed.

name: Ahmad Baba
line: A Timbuktu scholar carried off to Marrakesh after Morocco conquered Songhai.
story: From a family of scholars, he wrote over forty works, including a dictionary of Maliki scholars and a ruling against enslaving free Muslims of West Africa. After the Moroccan invasion of 1591 he was taken in chains to Marrakesh, where he taught until he was allowed home years later.
legacy: The Ahmed Baba Institute in Timbuktu, guardian of the city's manuscripts, bears his name.

name: Ebussuud Efendi
line: Suleiman's chief mufti, who worked to bring Ottoman state law into line with the Sharia.
story: As Shaykh al-Islam for nearly thirty years, he issued thousands of fatwas and harmonised Ottoman land and tax law with Hanafi law. He also wrote a respected tafsir, Irshad al-Aql al-Salim.
legacy: His fatwas guided Ottoman courts for centuries.

name: Katip Celebi
line: An Ottoman clerk whose catalogue lists some 14,500 books of the Islamic world.
story: He served as an army clerk before giving himself to study. His Kashf al-Zunun catalogues Arabic, Persian and Turkish books by subject, and his Cihannuma is a world geography that drew on European atlases too.
legacy: Kashf al-Zunun is still a starting point for the history of Islamic books.

name: Evliya Celebi
line: An Ottoman traveller whose ten-volume Book of Travels covers forty years on the road.
story: He wrote that in a dream of the Prophet ﷺ he meant to ask for intercession (shafa'ah) but asked for travel (siyahah) by mistake, and was granted both. He journeyed through the Balkans, Anatolia, the Caucasus, Persia, Egypt and Sudan, and his Seyahatname mixes careful description, humour and tall tales.
legacy: His book is a treasure-house on Ottoman cities and peoples.

name: Abu Ishaq al-Shatibi
role: Jurist of the aims of the Sharia
line: A Granada jurist who explained the higher aims behind Islamic law.
story: In al-Muwafaqat he argued that the Sharia exists to protect religion, life, intellect, lineage and property, and that rulings should be read in light of these aims. In al-I'tisam he wrote against innovations in worship.
legacy: Maqasid al-Shariah, now a major field of Islamic thought, leans heavily on his work.
note: Not the same person as al-Qasim al-Shatibi, the master of the Quran readings.

name: Muhammad al-Jazuli
line: A Moroccan Sufi whose book of blessings on the Prophet ﷺ is recited worldwide.
story: From the Sous in southern Morocco, he studied in Fez and wrote Dala'il al-Khayrat, a collection of prayers of blessing on the Prophet ﷺ, answering the Quran's call to bless him. It became one of the most copied books in the Muslim world. His tomb is in Marrakesh.
legacy: Dala'il al-Khayrat is still read in circles from Morocco to Malaysia.

name: Al-Maghili
line: A North African jurist whose advice shaped Islamic rule in Kano and the Songhai Empire.
story: He crossed the Sahara to advise the ruler of Kano and the Songhai king Askia Muhammad on just government, in letters still studied today. His replies to Askia's questions became a handbook for Muslim rulers in West Africa.
legacy: Later West African reformers, Usman dan Fodio among them, quoted him often.
note: He also led the destruction of a synagogue in Tuat, an act that other jurists of his time opposed.

name: Ahmad al-Tijani
line: An Algerian-born master whose order became one of the largest in West Africa.
story: Born in Ain Madhi in Algeria, he studied in Fez, Tunis, Cairo and Makkah, then settled in Fez under the sultan's protection. His order, the Tijaniyya, spread through traders and scholars across the Sahara.
legacy: Millions in Senegal, Nigeria and beyond follow the Tijaniyya today.

name: Usman dan Fodio
line: A Fulani scholar whose call for justice grew into the Sokoto Caliphate.
story: For decades he preached across Hausaland against corrupt rule and un-Islamic customs, and taught women alongside men. When the king of Gobir turned on his community, he made a hijrah in 1804, and the jihad that followed united the region under one caliphate. He left government to his son Muhammad Bello and brother Abdullahi and kept writing.
legacy: The Sokoto Caliphate and his many works in Arabic, Fulfulde and Hausa shaped northern Nigeria.
note: As the founder of the Sokoto Caliphate he may also appear among rulers.

name: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi
line: An Algerian scholar whose desert lodges spread learning and order across Libya and the Sahara.
story: After study in Fez and Makkah, he founded the Sanusiyya and built lodges (zawiyas) along the caravan routes of Cyrenaica. These lodges taught the Quran, farmed the land and settled tribal disputes.
legacy: The Sanusi network led Libyan resistance to Italian rule, and the Sanusi family later became Libya's royal house.

name: Nana Asma'u
line: Usman dan Fodio's daughter, who trained women teachers to carry learning to the villages.
story: Fluent in Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa and Tamasheq, she wrote poems on faith, history and medicine. She organised the 'yan taru', women teachers who travelled to rural women with her verse lessons.
legacy: The yan taru network still exists in northern Nigeria.

name: Uways al-Barawi
line: A Somali scholar who spread the Qadiri order and Arabic learning along the East African coast.
story: Born in Brava, he studied in Baghdad at the centre of the Qadiri order and returned to found communities of learning. His students carried the Qadiriyya to Zanzibar, Tanganyika and Congo. He was killed in 1909 in a raid by a rival movement.
legacy: His network helped root Islamic learning deep in the East African interior.

name: Habib Salih
line: A scholar from the Comoros whose Riyadha mosque in Lamu opened learning to the poor and freed slaves.
story: Of Hadrami descent and born in the Comoros, he settled in Lamu and founded the Riyadha mosque and college around 1900. He welcomed those the old elite had shut out, and his yearly Mawlid celebration drew pilgrims from across the coast.
legacy: The Riyadha mosque and Lamu's Maulidi festival continue his work.
note: Many details come from local tradition.
aliases: Habib Salih ibn Alawi Jamal al-Layl

name: Ahmadu Bamba
line: A Senegalese Sufi who resisted French rule without taking up arms.
story: His growing following alarmed the French, who exiled him to Gabon and Mauritania for years. He answered with prayer, work and thousands of verses of devotional poetry, and founded the town of Touba.
legacy: The Muridiyya and its yearly pilgrimage to Touba, the Grand Magal, draw millions.

name: Hamzah Fansuri
line: The first great poet of the Malay language, who wrote of God's love in Malay verse.
story: From Barus or nearby on the coast of Sumatra, he travelled to Arabia and Baghdad and wrote Sufi poems and prose in Malay. His verse form, the syair, became a lasting form of Malay poetry.
legacy: He made Malay a language of Islamic thought.
note: His dates are uncertain: some place his death around 1590, others, from a gravestone in Makkah, in 1527. His Sufi ideas were later condemned by al-Raniri.

name: Wang Daiyu
line: The first to explain Islam in the language of Confucian China.
story: Raised in a Muslim family of Nanjing, he studied Confucian, Buddhist and Daoist texts. His True Explanation of the Orthodox Teaching presented Islamic belief in terms Chinese scholars could follow.
legacy: He opened the 'Han Kitab', a library of Islamic works written in Chinese.

name: Nur al-Din al-Raniri
line: A Gujarati scholar who served the sultans of Aceh and wrote a great history of the world in Malay.
story: Born in Rander in Gujarat, he came to Aceh and wrote Bustan al-Salatin, an encyclopedic world history in Malay, for Sultan Iskandar Thani. He also wrote al-Sirat al-Mustaqim, a Malay manual of fiqh, and attacked the teachings of Hamzah Fansuri's followers.
legacy: His books shaped Malay Islamic writing for generations.

name: Abd al-Rauf al-Singkili
line: An Acehnese scholar who wrote the first complete tafsir of the Quran in Malay.
story: After some nineteen years of study in Arabia, he returned to Aceh and served as chief judge under a line of queens. His Tarjuman al-Mustafid was the first full Malay commentary on the Quran.
legacy: His students spread the Shattari order across Sumatra and Java.

name: Liu Zhi
line: Author of a Chinese life of the Prophet ﷺ and books explaining Islamic law and thought in Chinese.
story: He spent decades studying Arabic, Persian and the Confucian classics. His Tianfang Zhisheng Shilu is a life of the Prophet ﷺ, and Tianfang Dianli explains Islamic rites and law in Chinese terms.
legacy: His works are the high point of the Han Kitab tradition and are still read by Chinese Muslims.
note: His exact dates are uncertain.

name: Nawawi al-Bantani
line: A Javanese scholar in Makkah who taught a generation of Southeast Asian ulama.
story: Born in Banten on Java, he settled in Makkah and wrote many books in Arabic, including a tafsir, Marah Labid. His students went home to lead the pesantren schools of Java.
legacy: His books remain staples of the pesantren curriculum in Indonesia.

name: Ahmad Dahlan
line: A Yogyakarta preacher who founded Muhammadiyah, now running thousands of schools and hospitals.
story: After study in Makkah he founded Muhammadiyah in 1912 to purify practice and build modern schools, clinics and orphanages under Dutch rule. His wife Siti Walidah led its women's wing, Aisyiyah.
legacy: Muhammadiyah is one of the largest Muslim organisations in the world.

name: Hasyim Asy'ari
line: A Javanese scholar who founded Nahdlatul Ulama, the world's largest Muslim organisation.
story: Trained in Makkah, he led the Tebuireng pesantren in Jombang and in 1926 founded Nahdlatul Ulama to defend the traditional schools of law, creed and Sufism. In 1945 he called on Muslims to defend newly independent Indonesia against the returning colonial forces.
legacy: Nahdlatul Ulama counts tens of millions of members today.

name: Shihab al-Din Marjani
line: A Tatar scholar who wrote the history of the Volga Muslims and renewed learning in Kazan.
story: After about eleven years of study in Bukhara and Samarkand, he became imam of a Kazan mosque and taught. He wrote histories of the Volga Bulgars and Tatars and pressed the madrasas to widen their studies.
legacy: He is honoured as a father of modern Tatar Muslim scholarship.

name: Sayyid Ahmad Khan
line: A Delhi scholar who founded the college at Aligarh to give Indian Muslims a modern education.
story: After the 1857 uprising he set out to rebuild Muslim confidence under British rule. In 1875 he founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College, later Aligarh Muslim University, and wrote a commentary on the Quran.
legacy: Aligarh trained much of the Muslim leadership of British India.
note: His rationalist tafsir was rejected by many ulama of his day.

name: Muhammad Qasim Nanautawi
line: A scholar who co-founded the Deoband seminary after 1857 to keep Islamic learning alive.
