story: After the crushing of the 1857 uprising, he and his colleagues opened a madrasa in Deoband in 1866, funded by public donations rather than rulers. It taught the Quran, hadith and fiqh in a structured course.
legacy: Thousands of Deobandi madrasas across South Asia, Africa and Britain grew from it.

name: Muhammad Abduh
line: An Egyptian scholar and mufti who sought to renew Islamic thought and education.
story: A student of Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, he was exiled after the British occupation of 1882. Returning, he became Grand Mufti of Egypt and pushed for reform at al-Azhar. His Quran lessons were written up by his student Rashid Rida as Tafsir al-Manar.
legacy: His ideas shaped both modernist and revivalist movements of the 20th century.
note: Admirers saw a renewer; traditional critics felt he gave reason and modern ideas too much weight.

name: Marmaduke Pickthall
line: An English novelist who became Muslim and made one of the first English translations by a Muslim.
story: He declared his Islam in London in 1917 and later worked in Hyderabad for the Nizam. He took leave to consult scholars in Cairo, and published The Meaning of the Glorious Koran in 1930.
legacy: Still in print, it opened the Quran's meanings to English readers for a century.

name: Said Nursi
line: A Kurdish scholar who wrote the Risale-i Nur to defend faith in the secular Turkish republic.
story: Called Bediuzzaman, 'wonder of the age', he led volunteers in the First World War and was a prisoner in Russia. Under the new republic he was exiled and jailed for decades, yet wrote a vast commentary on faith, the Risale-i Nur, spread at first by hand-copying.
legacy: Millions in Turkey and beyond study the Risale-i Nur in reading circles.

name: Muhammad Iqbal
line: A poet-philosopher of Lahore who called Muslims to rediscover the self and their faith.
story: Educated in Lahore, Cambridge and Munich, he wrote poetry in Urdu and Persian urging Muslims to awaken. His lectures, The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam, engaged Western philosophy. In 1930 he proposed a Muslim homeland in north-west India.
legacy: He is Pakistan's national poet, and his poems are loved from Iran to Turkey.

name: Abd al-Hamid ibn Badis
line: An Algerian scholar who revived Arabic and Islamic schooling under French rule.
story: In Constantine he taught tafsir for decades, and in 1931 founded the Association of Algerian Muslim Ulema, which opened schools across the country. His motto was: 'Islam is our religion, Arabic our language, Algeria our homeland.'
legacy: His schools kept Arabic and Islamic identity alive through colonial rule.

name: Asad ibn al-Furat
role: Judge of Kairouan, conqueror of Sicily
line: A jurist of Kairouan who led the Muslim landing in Sicily at about seventy.
story: He studied with Malik in Madinah and with Abu Hanifa's students in Iraq, and his notes, the Asadiyyah, became the base of Sahnun's Mudawwana. As judge of Kairouan he was chosen to command the Aghlabid fleet that landed in Sicily in 827. He died during the siege of Syracuse.
legacy: Muslim Sicily, which lasted over two centuries, began with his landing.

name: Rashid al-Din
line: A physician and vizier of the Mongol Ilkhans who wrote the first true history of the world.
story: Born to a Jewish family of Hamadan, he became Muslim and rose as physician and then vizier to Ghazan Khan after Ghazan embraced Islam. His Jami' al-Tawarikh covers the Mongols, China, India, the Franks and the prophets. He built a whole quarter of learning in Tabriz, and was executed after court intrigues.
legacy: Its illustrated copies are treasures of Persian painting and a key source on the Mongols.

name: Qol Sharif
line: The chief imam of Kazan, who died with his students defending the city against Ivan the Terrible.
story: A scholar and poet who led the religious life of the Kazan Khanate, he fought at the head of his students when Russian forces stormed the city in 1552. He was killed in the fighting, and Kazan's mosques were destroyed.
legacy: The great mosque rebuilt in Kazan's kremlin in 2005 bears his name.

name: Ibrahim Muteferrika
line: A Hungarian-born convert who set up the first Turkish-language printing press in Istanbul.
story: Born in Transylvania, he came to Istanbul, became Muslim and served as a diplomat. With a fatwa and the sultan's permission he opened a press, printing its first book, an Arabic-Turkish dictionary, in 1729. He printed maps, histories and science, but not the Quran, which scribes still copied.
legacy: His press opened the way for printed books in the Ottoman lands.

name: Ayuba Suleiman Diallo
line: A Fulani scholar sold into slavery in Maryland who wrote out the Quran from memory and won his freedom.
story: The son of an imam in Bundu, in today's Senegal, he was captured and sold to a Maryland tobacco planter in 1731. A letter he wrote in Arabic reached England, where scholars recognised his learning. Freed and taken to London, he wrote out copies of the Quran from memory, and returned home in 1734.
legacy: His story is among the earliest records of enslaved African Muslims in the Americas.

name: Omar ibn Said
line: A West African scholar enslaved in North Carolina who wrote his life story in Arabic.
story: Educated for some twenty-five years in Futa Toro, he was captured in 1807 and shipped to Charleston. In 1831 he wrote a short autobiography in Arabic, opening it with Surah al-Mulk, which he knew by heart. He remained enslaved until his death.
legacy: His memoir is the only known autobiography in Arabic by an enslaved person in America.

name: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani
line: A restless preacher who travelled from India to Paris urging Muslims to unite against European rule.
story: He taught and agitated in Afghanistan, Istanbul, Cairo, Paris and Iran, calling Muslims to unity, reason and resistance to colonial power. In Paris in 1884 he and Muhammad Abduh published al-Urwa al-Wuthqa. He died in Istanbul under the eye of Sultan Abdul Hamid II.
legacy: His call for unity and reform echoed in later Islamic movements across the world.
note: He claimed Afghan birth, but most historians think he was born in Asadabad in Iran. His beliefs and politics are much debated.

name: Si Kaddour Benghabrit
line: An Algerian-born scholar and diplomat who founded the Grand Mosque of Paris and was its first rector.
story: Trained in Islamic law, he served the Moroccan sultans as a diplomat. The Grand Mosque of Paris, opened in 1926, honoured North African Muslims who died for France in the First World War. During the Nazi occupation the mosque is reported to have sheltered people in danger, including some Jews.
legacy: The Paris Mosque remains a centre of Muslim life in France.
note: How many people the mosque sheltered during the war is debated.

name: Hasan al-Banna
line: An Egyptian schoolteacher who founded the Muslim Brotherhood in 1928.
story: Teaching in Ismailia, near the British-run Suez Canal, he founded the Brotherhood to call people back to Islam through preaching, schools and welfare. It grew into a mass movement across Egypt and beyond. He was assassinated in Cairo in 1949.
legacy: The movement he founded spread across the Arab world.
note: His movement has been both admired and opposed; this entry records only the historical facts.

name: Mahmoud Khalil al-Husary
line: An Egyptian reciter who made the first complete recording of the Quran.
story: He memorised the Quran as a boy in his village and mastered the ten readings. Around 1961 he recorded the whole Quran in the steady murattal style, and later in other readings. His clear, careful recitation became the model for learners worldwide.
legacy: His recordings are still used to teach correct recitation.

name: Ibrahim ibn Adham
line: A prince of Balkh who, tradition says, gave up his throne to live by the work of his hands.
story: Stories tell that while hunting he heard a voice asking whether he was created for this, and he left his palace for a life of poverty. He worked as a harvester and gardener in Syria, refusing to eat anything not earned honestly, and died on the Byzantine frontier.
legacy: He became a model of renunciation for Sufis everywhere.
lesson: Honest earning and a free heart are worth more than a throne.
note: Most details come from later Sufi biographies.

name: Thabit ibn Qurra
line: A Sabian of Harran whose translations and mathematics enriched the House of Wisdom tradition.
story: Brought to Baghdad by Muhammad ibn Musa of the Banu Musa, he translated Greek works of Euclid, Archimedes and Ptolemy into Arabic. He found a rule for amicable numbers and wrote on the balance, astronomy and medicine.
legacy: His family of scholars served the Abbasid court for generations.
note: He remained a Sabian, a follower of the old star religion of Harran, and did not become Muslim.

name: Al-Mutanabbi
line: A poet of Kufa whose verses are counted the summit of classical Arabic poetry.
story: Born in Kufa, he wandered as a young man and was jailed for leading a revolt. At the Aleppo court of Sayf al-Dawla he wrote his finest praise of the Hamdanid wars against Byzantium. He was killed by bandits near Baghdad, reportedly after a line of his own poetry shamed him out of fleeing.
legacy: Arabic speakers still quote his lines as proverbs.
note: His nickname, 'the would-be prophet', is said to come from a claim made in his youth.

name: Firdawsi
line: A poet of Tus who spent some thirty years writing the Shahnameh, the epic of Persia's kings.
story: In about 50,000 couplets he retold the legends and history of Iran down to the Muslim conquest, using few Arabic words. He presented the poem to Mahmud of Ghazna, who, the story goes, rewarded him poorly.
legacy: The Shahnameh helped keep the Persian language alive as a language of Muslim culture.
note: The tale of Mahmud's meagre reward is a well-known legend.

name: Ali Hujwiri
line: A Sufi from Ghazni whose Kashf al-Mahjub is the oldest Sufi treatise in Persian.
story: After long travels through the Muslim lands he settled in Lahore. Kashf al-Mahjub, 'the Unveiling of the Veiled', explains the Sufi path and insists that it must keep to the Sharia.
legacy: His shrine in Lahore, Data Darbar, is one of the busiest in South Asia.

name: Al-Bakri
line: An Andalusian geographer whose book gives the earliest detailed picture of the Ghana Empire.
story: He never left al-Andalus, but gathered reports from merchants and travellers. His Book of Roads and Kingdoms (1068) describes Ghana's capital, with its Muslim quarter of twelve mosques beside the king's town.
legacy: Historians of West Africa still rely on his account.

name: Attar of Nishapur
role: Poet of the Conference of the Birds
line: A pharmacist-poet of Nishapur whose Conference of the Birds is a classic of the soul's journey.
story: He ran a pharmacy and wrote poetry in Persian. In the Conference of the Birds, thirty birds cross seven valleys seeking their king and find him in themselves, a parable of the search for God. His Memorial of the Saints gathers the lives of early Sufis.
legacy: Rumi honoured him as a master of the path.
note: Tradition says he was killed when the Mongols sacked Nishapur.

name: Abd al-Latif al-Baghdadi
line: A Baghdad physician whose eyewitness account of Egypt describes a terrible famine and the pyramids.
story: He met Salah al-Din and taught in Cairo and Damascus. In Egypt during the famine of 1200-1202 he examined many skeletons and found that Galen was wrong about the lower jaw. His account also describes the pyramids and the Sphinx.
legacy: His book is an early model of checking authorities against observation.

name: Shams Tabrizi
line: The wandering dervish of Tabriz whose friendship turned Rumi into a poet.
story: He arrived in Konya in 1244 and spent long months in conversation with Rumi, to the jealousy of Rumi's students. He left, returned, and around 1248 vanished for good. Rumi poured his grief and love into the poems of the Divan-i Shams.
legacy: Without him, the poetry of Rumi might never have been written.
note: What happened to him is unknown; some later stories say he was murdered, which historians doubt.

name: Hafiz
line: A poet of Shiraz whose lyrics are the most loved in the Persian language.
story: He took his pen-name from having memorised the Quran. His Divan of ghazals speaks of love, wine and longing in images that readers have long read as symbols of love for God. Many Persian homes keep a copy beside the Quran.
legacy: His tomb in Shiraz is a place of pilgrimage for poetry lovers.
note: Whether his imagery is spiritual or worldly has been debated for centuries.

name: Jami
line: A Naqshbandi poet and scholar of Herat, often called the last great classical Persian poet.
story: At the Timurid court of Herat he wrote seven long poems, the Haft Awrang, retelling stories such as Yusuf and Zulaykha, and Nafahat al-Uns, lives of the saints. He also wrote an Arabic grammar used in madrasas for centuries.
legacy: His Yusuf and Zulaykha was copied and illustrated across the Persian-speaking world.
note: The name Zulaykha for the Aziz's wife comes from later tradition, not the Quran.

name: Bihzad
line: The greatest master of Persian miniature painting, working in Herat and Tabriz.
story: He painted for the Timurid court of Herat, filling book pages with lively crowds, builders and gardens. After the Safavids took Herat he moved to Tabriz and directed the royal library workshop.
legacy: His style shaped Persian, Ottoman and Mughal painting.

name: Zayn al-Din al-Malibari
line: A scholar of Malabar who wrote a history calling Muslims to resist the Portuguese.
story: From a scholarly family of Ponnani in Kerala, he wrote Tuhfat al-Mujahidin, a history of Islam in Malabar and of Portuguese attacks on its ports. His Fath al-Mu'in is a Shafi'i law manual still studied across the Indian Ocean.
legacy: Fath al-Mu'in is a standard text from Kerala to Indonesia.
